about: A long reported piece for the harness, written for The Clearing's own tests (Nov 8, 2026). It has quotes, titles and times with periods, a stock lede and a sentence that runs long, so the note walk and Quick check can be looked at on a piece several screens tall. Fiction: no real people or places.
title: The last stop on Route 9
body:
In today's rapidly changing information landscape, rural libraries face hard choices, and the Harlow County bookmobile is no exception.

The bookmobile is a converted school bus, white with a green stripe, that has carried about four thousand books a week to eleven stops in the north end of the county since 1987. On the first Tuesday of December it will make its last run. The county commission voted 3 to 2 in October to sell the bus and put the money toward a new reading room at the main branch in Alder.

The last stop on the Tuesday route is the parking lot of the Grange hall in Pell, at 3:40 p.m. On a cold afternoon in November, eleven people were waiting for it, and four of them had walked.

One of them was Agnes Ruiz, who is eighty-one and has been coming to the Pell stop since her husband drove her there in a feed truck. She brought back six mysteries in a canvas bag and took out six more. She reads one a day, she said, two if it rains.

"I don't drive anymore," she said. "The library in Alder might as well be on the moon."

It is worth noting that Alder is twenty-six miles from Pell, and there is no bus.

The driver, Tom Okafor, has run the north route for nineteen years. He knows which patrons want large print and which ones want the newest thriller before anybody else has read it, and he keeps a list in a spiral notebook on the dash. He knows that the Hendersons' boy, who is eleven, reads only books about ships, and that Mrs. Lind at the Corley stop will not take a book with a torn cover.

"At the end of the day, we have to be good stewards of the resources this community has entrusted to us," said Dr. Ellen Marsh, the county's library director, in an interview in her office at the main branch, which looks out over the lot where the bookmobile parks at night. "Moving forward, we want to leverage our world-class facility to serve everyone."

Marsh said the bus costs about $61,000 a year to run, counting fuel, insurance, repairs and Okafor's salary. The new reading room will cost about $240,000 to build, and the county has applied for a state grant to cover most of it. State Sen. Ray Dunning, whose district includes Pell, wrote a letter supporting the grant.

"This is not a story about cutting a service, it's a story about building a better one," Marsh said. "Very few systems our size still run a bookmobile at all."

That is true. Of the nine county systems in the region, two still run one. Both have kept their routes by sharing a bus between counties, an arrangement Harlow County has never tried.

The commissioners who voted against the sale, Ann Pryor and Lou Bell, said the county should have asked the people on the route first. Pryor, whose district takes in most of the north end, held a meeting at the Grange hall in September. Forty people came on a weeknight, she said, in a town of three hundred.

"They asked me what kind of county we wanted to be," Pryor said. "I didn't have a good answer."

The bookmobile's own numbers are hard to read. Checkouts on the north route have fallen by about a third since 2015, the year the county put its catalog online, and Marsh pointed to that drop more than once. But the route's patrons are older than the county's, and many of them have no internet at home. When the county surveyed the route in 2022, more than half the people who answered said the bookmobile was the only way they got books at all.

Okafor keeps his own count. On the November afternoon in Pell he wrote down every patron by first name and the number of books each one took, the way he has every week since he started, in pencil, in a column down the left side of the page.

At 4:15 he closed the back door of the bus. Agnes Ruiz was still in the lot, her bag of six mysteries on the bench beside her, waiting for a neighbor who had promised to drive her home and who was by then forty minutes late, a delay she said was normal for him and which she did not seem to mind, since it gave her time to start the first book before the light went.

She was reading when the bus pulled out.

The commission will take up the grant in January. If it comes through, the reading room in Alder is expected to open in the fall of next year, with a children's corner, eight computers and a meeting room that seats sixty.

The bus will be sold at auction in the spring. Okafor said he has thought about bidding on it.

"I wouldn't know what to do with it," he said. "Drive it out to Pell, I guess, and park."
